VARIABLES
1. Assign the values 25, 50, and 100 to variables a, b, and c. Calculate their average and store it in a variable named average. Then, increase a by 10% (so that a becomes 27.5) and calculate the new average. Record the original and new averages, and explain the difference.
```{r}
a <- 25
b <- 50
c <- 100
(mn <- mean(a,b,c))
(mn1 <- mean((1.1*a),b,c))
mn1 - mn
```
The mean increased by the increase in the 25 (2.5).

2. Create two variables: product_cost set to 120 and selling_price set to 150. Calculate the profit margin percentage as (selling_price - product_cost) / product_cost * 100 and store it in a variable named profit_margin. Then, increase selling_price to 180 and calculate the new profit margin. Compare the initial and updated profit margins.
```{r}
product_cost <- 120
selling_price <- 150
(profit_margin <- (selling_price - product_cost) / product_cost * 100)
(profit_margin1 <- (180 - product_cost) / product_cost * 100)
```

3. Define a variable my_string with the sentence "I love playing the guitar." Use nchar(my_string) to count the number of characters in this sentence and store the result in a variable called char_count. Print both my_string and char_count together. Describe what you observe in the output.
```{r}
(my_string <- "I love playing the guitar.")
(char_count <- nchar(my_string))
```

4. Set a variable called initial_value to 10. Write a function double_value() that doubles initial_value and
returns the result. Call double_value() with initial_value as input and check if the original initial_value outside
the function has changed or not. Explain why it changed or didn’t change.
```{r}
initial_value <- 10
double_value <- function(x) 2*x
double_value(initial_value)
```

5. Write a function calculate_total() that takes item_price = 15 and quantity = 3 as arguments and returns the
total cost. Define a global variable tax_rate with a value of 0.1 (10%) and modify calculate_total() to include
tax in the total cost. Change tax_rate to 0.2 outside the function and call calculate_total() again. Observe
whether the total changes and explain why.
```{r}
calculate_total <- function(item_price = 15, quantity = 3) item_price*quantity
calculate_total()
```
```{r}
tax_rate <- 0.1
calculate_total2 <- function(item_price = 15, quantity = 3) item_price*quantity + (tax_rate*item_price*quantity)
calculate_total2()
```
```{r}
tax_rate <- 0.2
calculate_total2 <- function(item_price = 15, quantity = 3) item_price*quantity + (tax_rate*item_price*quantity)
calculate_total2()
```

6. Create a variable values with a list of numbers values <- c(5, 10, 15). Write a function that calculates both
the mean and standard deviation of the numbers in values without using mean() or sd(). Return both results
from the function. Compare your function’s results to R’s mean(values) and sd(values).
```{r}
values <- c(5, 10, 15)
mean_and_sd <- function(values){
  mn <- sum(values)/length(values)
  s_sq <- (values - mn)^2
  stan_dev <- sqrt(sum(s_sq)/(length(s_sq)-1))
  return(c(mn, stan_dev))
}
mean_and_sd(values)
```
```{r}
mean(values)
sd(values)
```

7. Set initial_investment to 1000 and define a global variable growth_rate with a value of 0.05 (5% annual
growth). Write a function investment_growth() that calculates the future value of the investment over 5 years.
Change growth_rate to 0.1 outside the function and call investment_growth() again. Observe and explain the
difference in results.
```{r}
initial_investment <- 1000
growth_rate <- 0.05
investment_growth <- function(years = 5) initial_investment*((1+growth_rate)^years)
investment_growth()
```
```{r}
initial_investment <- 1000
growth_rate <- 0.01
investment_growth <- function(years = 5) initial_investment*((1+growth_rate)^years)
investment_growth()
```

8. Set height to 10 and width to 5, representing the dimensions of a rectangle, and calculate the area as height * width. Then, redefine width as a function that returns height * 1.5 and recalculate the area using this function. Explain if redefining width as a function in this case is practical and why.
```{r}
height <- 10
width <- 5
area <- function(height, width) height*width
area(height, width)
```
```{r}
height <- 10
width <-  height * 1.5
area <- function(height, width) height*width
area(height, width)
```

9. Use a for-loop to create three variables, day1, day2, and day3, each assigned a random temperature value in Celsius (use values of 22, 24, and 19 for the temperatures). Calculate the average temperature across these days. Reflect on whether creating individual variables for each day is efficient if you wanted to store temperatures for 100 days instead. Suggest an alternative method.
```{r}
temperatures <- numeric(3)

for (i in 1:3) {
  if (i == 1) temperatures[i] <- 22
  if (i == 2) temperatures[i] <- 24
  if (i == 3) temperatures[i] <- 19
}
day1 <- temperatures[1]
day2 <- temperatures[2]
day3 <- temperatures[3]

average_temperature <- mean(temperatures)

print(paste("Day 1 temperature:", day1, "°C"))
print(paste("Day 2 temperature:", day2, "°C"))
print(paste("Day 3 temperature:", day3, "°C"))
print(paste("Average temperature:", round(average_temperature, 2), "°C"))
```

10. Create a variable named test_scores to store a list of five scores: 85, 90, 78, 92, 88. Write a function that
calculates the highest, lowest, and average score from this list. Test the function and explain how using a clear
name like test_scores improves the readability of the code and its purpose.
```{r}
test_scores <- c(85, 90, 78, 92, 88)
print(paste("The highest score is:", max(test_scores)))
print(paste("The lowest score is:", min(test_scores)))
print(paste("The average score is:", mean(test_scores)))
```

17. Write a recursive function factorial_recursive that calculates the factorial of a given number. Test it with n = 4 and confirm it returns 24.
```{r}
factorial_recursive <- function(n){
  if(n<0){
    return("n is negative")
  }
  if(n==0 | n==1){
    return(1)
  }else{
    return(n*factorial_recursive(n-1))
  }
}
factorial_recursive(3)
```

8. Write an if-else statement to check if a given year is a leap year. The rules are that the year is a leap year if it’s divisible by 4 but not by 100, except if it’s also divisible by 400. Test it with 2020, 1900, and 2000 to confirm it returns the correct result each time.
```{r}
is_leap <- function(x){
  if((x%%4 == 0 && x %% 100 != 0) | (x%%400 == 0)){

  }else{
    return(FALSE)
  }
}

is_leap(1900)
is_leap(2000)
```

```{r}
moving_average <- function(vec, n){
  res <- c()
  i<-1
  while(i+(n-1)<=length(vec)){
    b <- mean(vec[i:(i+(n-1))])
    i<-i+1
    res <- c(res, b)
  }
  return(res)
}

```

  n <- length(vec1)

  }
